newsitem.title: USA: Democrats vow fight over Republican welfare plan.
newsitem.headline: Democrats vow fight over Republican welfare plan.

text.p: The White House and congressional Democrats Wednesday accused Republicans of violating a balanced budget deal protecting federal benefits for disabled legal immigrants, promising a tough fight.

Michigan Democratic Rep. Sander Levin also criticized provisions of a new Republican bill that essentially overturn a White House policy applying minimum wage laws to welfare recipients enrolled in workfare programs.

"(This measure) would not only break the budget agreement but break the backs of tens of thousands of legal immigrants," Levin said. "This bill is heading toward confrontation instead of bipartisan accord."

Vice President Al Gore issued a statement late Tuesday calling the Republican bill, which would deny future aid to thousands of legal immigrants who become disabled, "harsh, unfair and unecessary" and said it violated the budget deal.
The legislation, to be voted on by a House subcommittee Friday, is needed to implement part of a five-year balanced budget deal worked out by Republicans and the White House.
A landmark welfare law signed by President Clinton last year ends federal benefits to most legal immigrants this summer. But Clinton won major concessions in the budget agreement to "fix" the law.

Under the original budget, legal immigrants who were in the United States by Aug. 22, 1996, and were either on the rolls because of disability or became disabled in the future could receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Medicaid.

Immigrants who were receiving SSI benefits because they were elderly and impoverished, rather than disabled, would have been cut off. Estimates were that about 20 percent of 700,000 immmigrants receiving SSI would lose aid.
Under the new Republican plan all legal immigrants -- including the elderly poor -- receiving SSI on Aug. 22, 1996, could continue to get aid.
Legal immigrants who were in the country on that date, but not on the rolls, would not be eligible for assistance even if they became disabled in the future.
Immigrants who had official sponsors with incomes above 150 percent of the poverty line, about $25,000 for a family of four, would lose benefits.
The White House estimated that 100,000 disabled immigrants would lose benefits under the new Republican plan, due to the income test.

Republican Rep. Clay Shaw called his new plan more humane. He said under the original budget deal immigrants could have lost benefits for months while their cases were reconsidered and many elderly immigrants would lose benefits entirely.
The Florida Republican added that sponsors of legal immigrants, not the government, should take care of them.
"The federal government is not taking responsibility for disabilities of immigrants who come to the United States after possage of the welfare reform bill," Shaw said.
The new bill would require new immigrants to sign a pledge acknowledging that if they become a public charge, it would be grounds for deportation.
Shaw said Republicans were not looking to deport anyone, however aides said additional language on deportation would likely be added to the bill as it moves through the House.

The bill softens a White House ruling that welfare recipients in work programs qualify for the minimum wage. Many state governors have complained that requiring minimum wage would make welfare programs too expensive to implement.
It exempts some public and non-profit jobs from minimum wage. States could not require recipients to work more hours than the combined value of Food Stamps and cash benefits.

States could also count child care, housing and medical benefits when calculating work assignments, basically requiring welfare recipients to work off all benefits. The welfare law requires states to move half their recipients to work by the year 2002.
In one area of bipartisan agreement, the legislation includes $3 billion in grants to help create jobs in impoverished regions of the country.
